To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exercise training in miniature swine increases lipolytic sensitivity in the presence of energy restriction but not in the presence of excess energy intake.
the lipolytic response in vivo is not a simple reflection of the in vitro lipolytic response.
exercise training and energy intake interact in a manner that influences the cellular mechanisms regulating adipocyte lipolysis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of exercise and diet on the cellular mechanisms regulating adiposity and adipose tissue metabolism in swine.
elucidating the mechanisms that regulate adipose tissue lipolysis in response to energy intake and energy expenditure in a large mammal model.
the cellular and molecular adaptations in fat cells of miniature swine that are subjected to exercise training and/or excess energy intake.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cellular adaptations of adipocytes in response to exercise are dependent on energy intake.
the exercise training-induced lipolytic sensitivity was attenuated by energy excess.
the exercise-induced lipolysis is blunted by the excess energy intake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exercise training is an effective strategy for improving the health of obese subjects but only if energy intake is reduced.
excess energy intake blunts the lipolytic effects of exercise training, even if accompanied with exercise training.
exercise training in miniature pigs is a good model of human exercise training.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic response to exercise training in adipocytes is dependent on the energy intake of the swine.
exercise alone is not enough.
excess energy intake, even in the face of exercise training, can blunt the lipolytic response of fat tissue.
